Binary addition follows a single rule: 1+1 carries to the next column, exactly like decimal carrying — but with only two digits instead of ten.
puzzles.go_deeper: Write the numbers 0–7 in binary, then examine each adjacent pair: how many bits differ between consecutive numbers? You have discovered the Gray code — a sequence where adjacent numbers differ in exactly one binary digit. Where might this be useful? Hint: think about a dial that turns and what goes wrong if two bits change at once.
puzzles.silent_lesson: Positional notation; base-2 arithmetic; place value; binary addition and carrying; the universality of positional systems.

puzzles.title: The Speeding-Up Curve
puzzles.hook: A ball rolls down a ramp. At each second you measure how far it has travelled. The distances keep changing — but is there a number that captures exactly how fast it is moving at any single instant?
puzzles.challenge: Use this table of a moving object: time (s) = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; distance (m) = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Compute the average speed across each 1-second interval (distance gained ÷ time elapsed). Plot time vs average speed and notice the pattern. Now estimate the speed at exactly t = 2 s by shrinking the interval: t=2 to t=3, then t=2 to t=2.5, then t=2 to t=2.1, then t=2 to t=2.01. What value do the average speeds approach? Can you state a rule: if distance = t², what is the speed at any time t?
puzzles.discover: As the time interval shrinks toward zero, the average speed approaches a precise limit — 2t at any time t. You have found the derivative without being told its name. The rate of change of t² is exactly 2t at every instant. The key insight is the limit: not what happens at a single instant (which gives 0/0), but what value the ratio approaches as the interval becomes arbitrarily small.
puzzles.go_deeper: Try the same process for distance = t³: compute average speeds across shrinking intervals near t = 2 and t = 3. What rule do you find? Can you conjecture a general rule for tⁿ? Check whether distance = t⁴ follows the same pattern.
puzzles.silent_lesson: The derivative as a limit; average vs instantaneous rate of change; the power rule discovered empirically; limit concept; tangent as limiting secant.

puzzles.title: The Product Rule from First Principles
puzzles.hook: Two quantities are each changing. Their product is also changing — but at what rate? The answer is not simply the product of the two rates. Derive the exact rule.
puzzles.challenge: Let f and g be two functions of x. The product is P(x) = f(x)·g(x). Use the limit definition of the derivative to find P'(x): (1) Write P(x+h) − P(x) = f(x+h)·g(x+h) − f(x)·g(x). (2) Add and subtract f(x+h)·g(x) inside the expression. (3) Factor into two groups. (4) Divide by h and take the limit as h→0. (5) State the result. Now write the same result in both d/dx notation (d/dx[f·g] = ...) and in prime notation (fg)' = f'g + fg'. Finally, interpret each term geometrically: if f and g are the two sides of a rectangle whose area is P = f·g, what does each term in the rule represent?
puzzles.discover: The product rule d/dx[f·g] = f'g + fg' has a clean geometric meaning: the rate of growth of a rectangle's area equals (rate of growth of width × current height) + (current width × rate of growth of height). Both terms are needed because both sides are changing simultaneously. The algebraic derivation makes this precise via the limit; Leibniz's notation d/dx[fg] = g·df/dx + f·dg/dx makes the symmetry visible in a way that prime notation hides.
puzzles.go_deeper: Using the product rule, derive the quotient rule d/dx[f/g] by writing f/g = f·(g⁻¹) and applying the product rule together with the chain rule for g⁻¹. Then derive the power rule for negative integers: d/dx[x⁻ⁿ] = −n·x⁻ⁿ⁻¹. At each step identify which rule you are applying and why.
puzzles.silent_lesson: Limit definition of the derivative; product rule; Leibniz notation vs prime notation; geometric interpretation of differentiation rules; proof structure in calculus.

thinkers.name: Thomas Hobbes
thinkers.domain: Social Contract / Nature of Power / Leviathan

puzzles.title: The No-Rules Room
puzzles.hook: Your classroom has always had rules. What would happen if — just for five minutes — there were none at all? Would things get better, or worse?
puzzles.challenge: Round 1 — No rules: students are told there are no rules for 3 minutes. Record everything that happens — who takes what, whether anyone can work, what conflicts arise, whether anyone feels unsafe. Round 2 — Minimal rules: the class agrees on the three most essential rules and runs for another 3 minutes. Compare: (1) What was possible in Round 1 that became impossible in Round 2? (2) What was impossible in Round 1 that became possible in Round 2? (3) Which round felt safer? Which felt freer? Write your observations honestly — both rounds should reflect what actually happened, not what you expected.
puzzles.materials: Classroom space, paper and pencil for recording observations
puzzles.discover: Without rules, stronger or louder individuals tend to dominate; others cannot guarantee safety or access. With minimal agreed rules, everyone gains something — even those who lose some freedom gain security and predictability. The trade is real: give up unlimited freedom, gain reliable protection. Neither round is obviously better — the interesting question is which costs are worth which gains.
puzzles.go_deeper: Not all rules are equally important. Rank your Round 2 rules by asking: which rule, if broken just once, causes the most damage? Which can be broken occasionally without collapse? Rules that protect safety tend to rank higher than rules about fairness or procedure. What does this ordering reveal about what rules are fundamentally for?
puzzles.silent_lesson: State of nature; social contract as trade of freedom for security; rule of law; the difference between freedom and security; why individuals voluntarily accept constraints.

puzzles.title: Rules for the Stranded Five
puzzles.hook: Five people are stranded on an island with limited food and no outside help. They could cooperate — or fight. You have to design the minimal set of rules that makes cooperation possible.
puzzles.challenge: Situation: 5 people, one food source producing enough for 3 people per day, indefinitely. Without rules: each person is equally capable of taking all the food by force, but fighting wastes energy and risks injury. Your task: design a minimal rule-set (no more than 5 rules) that (1) keeps all five people alive long-term, (2) can be enforced without outside authority, (3) gives each person a reason to comply rather than defect. For each rule state: who enforces it, and what the penalty for violation is. Then identify which rules are self-enforcing (compliance is in everyone's interest regardless of others) and which require a designated enforcer. Finally: what happens if the designated enforcer themselves violates the rules?
puzzles.discover: Rules that are purely self-enforcing are more stable than rules requiring a trusted enforcer — because they don't create a privileged position that can be abused. But scarcity creates a coordination problem that pure self-interest alone cannot solve. The hardest problem is the enforcer problem: whoever enforces the rules also has the power to abuse them. This is the central puzzle of political authority, and there is no clean solution.
puzzles.go_deeper: Redesign your rule-set for a different situation: now there is enough food for all five, but it requires collective effort to harvest — and anyone can free-ride. How do the optimal rules change? Which type of scarcity (not enough even with cooperation, vs enough only if all cooperate) produces more or less stable social arrangements, and why?
puzzles.silent_lesson: Minimal rule design; coordination problems; enforcement and the enforcer problem; self-enforcing vs authority-dependent rules; political authority and its basis.

puzzles.title: Does Enforcement Make Agreements Possible?
puzzles.hook: A famous argument holds that in the absence of a power capable of enforcing agreements, all agreements will eventually break down — because rational actors will always defect when defection pays. Formalise this claim and find where it fails.
puzzles.challenge: Model the claim using the Prisoner's Dilemma. Payoff matrix: mutual cooperation = (3,3); mutual defection = (1,1); one defects while other cooperates = (5,0). (1) Show that defection is the dominant strategy in a single-shot game — regardless of what the other player does, defecting pays better. Write the dominance argument formally. (2) Now consider the iterated version (repeated indefinitely, both players remember history): does the dominant strategy change? Why? (3) Identify three real-world conditions under which agreements are maintained without a central enforcer. (4) State precisely where the original claim fails: is it always false, or only false under specific identifiable conditions?
puzzles.materials: Paper, pencil, payoff matrix drawn out
puzzles.discover: In a single-shot game, the claim holds: defection dominates and no agreement is stable without enforcement. In iterated games, cooperation can emerge through reciprocity — but only when future interactions are sufficiently valuable, players can identify each other, and defection can be detected and punished. The original claim fails exactly when these three conditions hold: repeated interaction, identifiability, and detectability. International trade agreements and long-term business relationships work precisely because these conditions are partially met.
puzzles.go_deeper: Axelrod's tournament (1980) showed that Tit-for-Tat wins iterated Prisoner's Dilemma tournaments: cooperate first, then mirror the other player's last move. Analyse why this strategy is robust: it is never the first to defect (nice), it retaliates immediately (punishing), and it forgives after one round (not vindictive). Design a modified strategy that beats Tit-for-Tat in at least one environment, and identify the conditions under which your modification succeeds.
puzzles.silent_lesson: Prisoner's Dilemma; dominant strategy; iterated games and cooperation; conditions for enforcement-free agreement; game theory formalisation of political philosophy; Hobbesian state of nature revisited.
